[Q3]: They refuse voluntary hair-cuts and sue in foreign commercial courts (e.g., New York, London), seizing debtor sovereign assets abroad to extort full payment.

The structural insolvency and debt overhang confronting the Global South represents a foundational crisis in international macroeconomic governance, sovereign finance law, and developmental ethics. Economists analyze the 'debt-climate trap,' demonstrating that climate-vulnerable states face sovereign credit rating downgrades, increasing their cost of capital precisely when extensive adaptation investments are required. In legal jurisprudence, sovereign debt workouts remain fragmented due to the absence of a statutory international bankruptcy mechanism analogous to Chapter 9 or Chapter 11. Private commercial creditors exploit collective action clause (CAC) thresholds and cross-default covenants to hold out from G20 Common Framework restructurings. Resolving this crisis requires establishing a multilateral sovereign debt workout mechanism under United Nations auspices, incorporating mandatory climate-resilient debt clauses (CRDCs) that automatically pause debt service during natural disasters, and passing statutory anti-vulture fund legislation in major financial jurisdictions.
Insolvency: The inability of a sovereign state or debtor to pay its debts or debt service obligations as they fall due.
Overhang: A condition where a nation's existing debt is so large that any extra income generated merely goes to paying creditors.
Covenant: A formal, binding legal agreement, promise, or condition written into a commercial contract or sovereign bond indenture.
Jurisprudence: The systematic philosophy, legal doctrines, and regulatory governance of law and justice.

Global E-Waste Justice & Right-to-Repair Supply Chains
Society & Global Issues

Open your old bedroom desk drawer: sitting in the back is a broken tablet and a tangled electronic wire with tiny bits of real gold and copper inside! When old electronics are tossed in the trash, they are often shipped overseas where workers burn plastic over an open campfire to extract metals, breathing toxic fumes. Instead of dumping electronics, every consumer deserves a legal Right to Repair so we can easily fix broken gadgets!

Creating an ethical electronics system requires manufacturers to use standard screws, provide free repair manuals, and sell inexpensive replacement batteries. Schools and neighborhood workshops host community fixing days where students learn how to solder wires and replace broken screens safely. To champion sustainable technology, students author a Circular Electronics and Right-to-Repair Pact featuring repairability scorecards and recycling rules!
Drawer: A box-shaped storage compartment without a lid, made to slide horizontally in and out of a desk or chest.
Wire: A slender, flexible thread or rod of metal used to carry electric current and signals inside electronic gadgets.
Campfire: An open outdoor fire at a camp or scrap yard, dangerous when used to burn toxic electronic plastics.

The global accumulation of electronic waste (e-waste) and the informal recycling of toxic electronics represents an acute environmental injustice and public health emergency. Worldwide, over 60 million metric tons of e-waste are generated annually, with significant volumes illicitly exported from developed countries to informal scrap yards in the Global South under the guise of 'used goods.' In these informal scrap yards, impoverished workers, including children, use open-air wire burning and toxic acid baths to extract trace gold and copper, exposing themselves and their communities to deadly levels of lead, mercury, and chlorinated dioxins. Resolving this crisis requires structural interventions: enforcing the Basel Convention to close export loopholes, mandating Design-for-Disassembly in electronics engineering, and codifying comprehensive 'Right to Repair' legislation that obligates manufacturers to supply standardized spare parts, diagnostic software, and repair schematics to independent technicians at reasonable prices.
Informal: Describing an unregulated, unofficial economic sector where workers lack legal protections, contracts, or safety gear.
Illicitly: In a way that is contrary to or forbidden by statutory law, international treaties, or official rules.
Loophole: An ambiguity or inadequacy in the law or a set of rules that allows someone to evade compliance or regulation.
Schematic: A technical diagram, blueprint, or plan showing the electrical connections and components of an electronic circuit.

The transboundary flow and informal pyrometallurgical processing of waste electrical and electronic equipment (WEEE) constitutes a critical nexus of environmental toxicology, circular materials engineering, and international trade law. Toxicologists trace the biological bioaccumulation of polybrominated diphenyl ethers (PBDEs) and neurotoxic heavy metals in informal e-waste communities, demonstrating severe pediatric neurological deficits and DNA hypermethylation. In product engineering, overcoming planned obsolescence demands enforcing eco-design criteria, such as scoring devices via standardized Repairability Indices and establishing mandatory 10-year firmware backwards compatibility. Legally, closing transboundary dumping channels requires reforming the Basel Convention on the Control of Transboundary Movements of Hazardous Wastes, removing the 'functional second-hand' exemption that facilitates the dumping of non-functional electronic waste in developing nations. Furthermore, just transition economics dictates formalizing informal scrap workers into certified, protective-gear urban mining cooperatives.
Toxicology: The branch of science concerned with the nature, effects, and detection of poisons and toxic chemical pollutants.
Obsolescence: The condition of being no longer useful, competitive, or functional because of newer alternatives or intentional design limits.
Transboundary: Crossing or situated across political, regional, or national territorial boundaries between sovereign countries.
Cooperative: An autonomous association of workers united voluntarily to meet their common economic and social needs through a jointly owned enterprise.

Ending Hidden Micronutrient Hunger Globally
Society & Global Issues

Look at a steaming bowl of fluffy white rice: it fills your tummy and gives you energy to play tag, providing plenty of daily food calorie energy! But a diet made solely of plain rice can lack essential micronutrients, causing invisible hidden hunger. Our growing bodies need tiny amounts of iron to carry oxygen through our bloodstream and zinc to boost our immune systems and heal scraped knees quickly.

Ending hidden hunger requires agricultural scientists, rural farmers, and neighborhood cooks to work together. Farmers plant golden sweet potatoes and biofortified zinc-rich grain, while local flour mills mix healthy vitamins into everyday staples. In our health unit, students construct a Nutrition Security and Biofortified Foodways Plan featuring nutritious school meal menus, home garden plans, and village flour fortification guidelines!
Calorie: A unit of energy used to measure the amount of energy our bodies get from eating food.
Iron: An essential mineral element that human red blood cells need to carry oxygen all through the body.
Zinc: A vital dietary mineral that helps the human immune system fight off viruses and heals cuts on our skin.
What is 'hidden hunger', and why does eating plain white rice not always give children all the vitamins they need?

[Q1]: Hidden hunger occurs when food provides caloric energy but lacks essential micronutrients like iron, zinc, and vitamin A.
[Q2]: Orange sweet potatoes are naturally rich in beta-carotene, which the human body converts into vitamin A to protect eyesight and fight off infections.
[Q3]: 6 packets × 6 days = 36 vitamin packets delivered.
[Activity]: Drawings should show a colorful variety of fruits and vegetables; rules should encourage eating at least three different colors of food each day.

Eradicating hidden micronutrient hunger represents one of the most critical public health, biochemical, and agricultural missions in global development. Over two billion people worldwide suffer from chronic micronutrient deficiencies—specifically insufficient intake of iron, zinc, iodine, and vitamin A. Unlike acute starvation, hidden hunger does not always manifest in emaciation, yet it silently stunts cognitive development, compromises immune system vitality, and increases maternal mortality. Combating this requires a multifaceted agronomic and industrial approach. Agronomists deploy conventional and marker-assisted biofortification to breed staple crops with elevated micronutrient concentrations, such as high-iron pearl millet, zinc-enriched rice, and beta-carotene-dense orange-fleshed sweet potatoes. Simultaneously, governments must support public-private partnerships that fortify staple foods—such as adding iodine to salt and vitamin A to cooking oil—at centralized regional food processing mills.
Deficiency: A lack or shortage of something essential, especially vital vitamins and minerals needed for human health.
Biofortification: The process of breeding crops to naturally increase their nutritional value through selective breeding or biotechnology.
Staple: A basic food that is eaten regularly and in such quantities as to constitute a dominant portion of a standard diet.
Millet: A fast-growing cereal plant grown in warm countries and dry regions that produces small, nutritious edible seeds.

[Q1]: Iron is the core cofactor of hemoglobin; deficiency causes anemia, reducing cerebral oxygen delivery and stunting neural dendrite development.
[Q2]: Selects for enhanced root zinc-transporter gene expression (OsZIP family) that mobilizes and translocates zinc ions directly into the rice grain endosperm.
[Q3]: Fortifying centralized processing mills reaches entire populations universally without requiring behavioral dietary changes, costing mere pennies per person.
[Q4]: ₱84,000 ÷ 3 = ₱28,000. Net budget = ₱28,000 - ₱2,800 = ₱25,200 per micronutrient security division.
[Rubric]: The policy must establish strict nutrient concentration benchmarks (ppm), mandatory testing at packaging mills, and dedicated farmer seed subsidies.

The global eradication of hidden hunger intersects human metabolic biochemistry, molecular crop physiology, and institutional food governance. Nutritional biochemists analyze the biological bioavailability of micronutrients, investigating how anti-nutritional factors like phytic acid chelate essential cations (Fe2+, Zn2+) in the human digestive tract, preventing intestinal absorption. Overcoming this requires engineering crops with reduced phytate-to-mineral molar ratios alongside scaling biofortification through CRISPR-directed genetic upregulation of ferritin and nicotianamine synthase. In public health economics, randomized controlled trials demonstrate that eliminating micronutrient deficits yields substantial macroeconomic returns, increasing adult wage earning capacity and reducing healthcare expenditures. Systemic policy implementation requires establishing mandatory statutory fortification standards for staple commodities, subsidizing smallholder farmer adoption of biofortified germplasm, and integrating nutrition security directly into primary healthcare protocols.
Bioavailability: The proportion of a nutrient, mineral, or drug that enters the body's circulation and is able to have an active biological effect.
Chelate: A chemical compound in which a metal ion is bound within a ring-like molecule, often preventing bodily absorption.
Ferritin: A universal intracellular protein that stores iron and releases it in a controlled fashion to prevent toxicity and deficiency.
Germplasm: Living genetic resources, such as seeds or tissues, maintained for the purpose of plant breeding and conservation.
Explain how phytic acid acts as an anti-nutritional factor by chelating divalent cations in the human gastrointestinal tract.

Evaluate the cultural foodways dilemma: How can public health agencies encourage adoption of biofortified crops without undermining indigenous culinary traditions?

Draft an executive legislative bill establishing mandatory fortification standards for commercial flours and oils, dedicated sovereign funding for biofortified seed dissemination, and free micronutrient testing in rural clinics.

[Q2]: Nicotianamine acts as an endogenous chelator, facilitating long-distance phloem transport of transition metals from leaves directly into seed tissues.
[Q3]: Imposes legal quality standards (e.g., minimum 30 mg/kg iron in flour), enforced via unannounced mill inspections and revocation of commercial licenses.
[Q4]: Must partner with local cooks and community elders to breed varieties that match preferred cooking textures, aromas, and traditional culinary recipes.
[Q5]: Year 1 = 400 × 1.15 = 460 co-ops. Year 2 = 460 × 1.12 = 515.2 (515 cooperatives). Total increase = 115.2 cooperatives (+28.8%).
[Rubric]: The legislative bill must feature statutory fortification minimums, independent chemical assay auditing, and dedicated smallholder farmer subsidies.

Today, software engineers can feed an old voice message and photo collection into an AI computer program to create an interactive digital avatar called a griefbot. While hearing an AI mimic a loved one's voice might feel comforting for a moment, an artificial program can never replace a true human soul.

Honoring our ancestors means holding their true memories close to our hearts through family stories, photo albums, and acts of loving remembrance. Communities establish digital privacy laws requiring personal permission before any likeness can be recreated digitally. Bereavement psychologists warn that while conversational avatars may offer temporary solace to grieving individuals, they can also disrupt the natural trajectory of bereavement, inducing chronic emotional denial, prolonged grief disorder, and unhealthy parasocial attachments to artificial constructs. Philosophically, an algorithm trained on archived texts and voice recordings produces mere statistical behavioral mimicry, lacking conscious intentionality or personal identity. In jurisprudence, the emergence of the 'digital afterlife' demands establishing clear posthumous privacy rights. Citizens must possess the legal right to execute a 'Digital Last Will,' specifying whether their personal correspondence, voice data, and likeness may be synthesized post-mortem. Crucially, consumer protection regulations must ban exploitative monetization, such as subscription paywalls or commercial advertising inside bereavement software.

Posthumous: Occurring, awarded, or appearing after the death of the originator or person.

The Ethics of Geoengineering: Modifying Earth's Sky
Philosophy & Religion

Look up at the endless blue sky: high above the clouds, our atmosphere filters sunlight and keeps our planet at a comfortable temperature. But as global warming increases, some scientists propose spraying a fine white aerosol mist into the upper stratosphere to create a planetary sunshade that reflects sunlight back into space. While dimming the sun might cool the Earth quickly, it could disrupt monsoon rains and cause sudden crop failures.

Altering the atmosphere of the entire planet affects all eight billion people on Earth, so no single nation has the right to modify the global sky unilaterally. World leaders, scientists, and citizens must maintain strict moratoriums against risky outdoor tests and focus on ending greenhouse emissions. To protect our common sky, students draft a Planetary Geoengineering Moratorium and Governance Treaty establishing strict international oversight and scientific research bans!
Sky: The region of the atmosphere and outer space seen from the Earth, shared by all living creatures.
Sunshade: A screen, canopy, or particle layer used to provide shade and block intense sunlight and heat.
Aerosol: A suspension of fine solid particles or liquid droplets in the air or atmosphere, like reflective sulfate mist.

The prospect of deploying solar radiation management (SRM)—specifically stratospheric aerosol injection (SAI) to deliberately cool the Earth—presents one of the most contentious dilemmas in environmental ethics, atmospheric physics, and global governance. Proponents argue that injecting reflective sulfur dioxide or calcium carbonate aerosols into the stratosphere could rapidly lower global temperatures, suppressing extreme heatwaves and polar ice melt while decarbonization efforts scale. However, climatologists model profound systemic risks: artificial solar dimming would alter global hydrological cycles, potentially disrupting the South Asian and West African monsoons upon which billions depend for agriculture. Furthermore, if an ongoing aerosol injection program were suddenly halted due to war or technical failure, the planet would face 'termination shock'—catastrophic rapid warming occurring in mere years. Crucially, solar geoengineering presents an acute moral hazard, potentially weakening political resolve to achieve deep industrial decarbonization.
Stratospheric: Situated within or relating to the stratosphere, the atmospheric layer 10 to 50 km above Earth containing the ozone layer.
Aerosol: A suspension of microscopic solid particles or liquid droplets in a gas, such as sulfate mists in the upper sky.
Monsoon: A seasonal prevailing wind in South and Southeast Asia, blowing from the southwest and bringing vital heavy rains.
Termination: The abrupt end or halting of an ongoing process, such as suddenly stopping an engineered solar shading program.

[Q3]: Without aerosol masking, decades of accumulated greenhouse heat would unmask within years, causing temperature spikes far too rapid for species to adapt.

The potential deployment of solar radiation management (SRM) constitutes an unprecedented crisis across stratospheric photochemistry, atmospheric dynamics, and public international law. Stratospheric chemical models evaluate catalytic ozone destruction, analyzing how surface reactions of hydrogen chloride and chlorine nitrate on engineered alumina or sulfate aerosols accelerate polar ozone depletion. Dynamically, radiative transfer equations model shortwave solar attenuation versus longwave terrestrial trapping, revealing that SRM compensates for radiative forcing without rectifying ocean acidification caused by ongoing anthropogenic CO2 emissions. In political philosophy and global justice, SRM exposes the profound fragility of global governance: a single unilateral actor with heavy aircraft could set Earth's planetary thermostat. Establishing an international regulatory architecture under the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) requires codifying a precautionary moratorium on outdoor deployment, accompanied by stringent international oversight of computer modeling.
Photochemistry: The branch of chemistry concerned with the chemical effects of light, particularly ultraviolet radiation on atmospheric molecules.
Attenuation: The gradual loss in intensity or amplitude of an electromagnetic flux (like sunlight) through absorption and scattering.
Acidification: The ongoing decrease in the pH of the Earth's oceans, caused primarily by the uptake of anthropogenic carbon dioxide from the air.
Unilateral: An action or decision performed by a single state or entity without the consultation or agreement of the international community.

Meaning, Purpose & Human Craft in Automated Abundance
Philosophy & Religion

Imagine an extraordinary future world where intelligent robots cultivate food, build comfortable homes, and clean our streets, creating a society of material abundance! Without the burden of exhausting daily chores, what will bring purpose and joy to human life? True fulfillment comes from artistic creativity, mastering new skills, and helping our neighbors. In community maker spaces, people gather in a sunny workshop to carve a wooden guitar, sculpt clay bowls, or practice gardening.

A post-automation society will celebrate caring, teaching, and human artistry above mechanical efficiency. Schools will transform into creative studios where students write poetry, plant community orchards, and solve environmental challenges alongside inspiring mentors. To envision this inspiring future, our young philosophers author a Post-Automation Human Flourishing Manifesto outlining community craft guilds and lifelong creative learning programs!
Abundance: A very large quantity of something, especially having plenty of food, goods, and resources for everyone.
Workshop: A room or building where goods are manufactured or created by hand, like woodworking or painting studios.
Guitar: A stringed musical instrument played with one's fingers or a pick, bringing joy and creativity to life.

As advanced artificial intelligence and autonomous robotics automate routine cognitive and physical labor, society confronts a profound philosophical and economic question: how will humans find purpose, mastery, and social identity in an era of technological abundance? For centuries, human dignity and social belonging have been tied directly to traditional wage labor and economic productivity. However, classical philosophers like Aristotle pointed to 'schole'—true leisure dedicated to intellectual contemplation, civic service, and creative mastery—as the highest human pursuit. In a post-labor society, public education must transition away from vocational training toward maker education, tactile craftsmanship, and civic participation. Economically, governments must establish universal basic dividends funded by automation dividends, ensuring that economic security is decoupled from wage employment and that all citizens possess the leisure and agency to cultivate human flourishing.
Contemplation: The action of looking thoughtfully at something, or deep reflective thought on philosophy, science, and the universe.
Vocational: Directed toward a specific occupation, trade, or career in the commercial job market.
Flourishing: A state of optimal human well-being, personal growth, happiness, and active civic contribution.
Abundance: An overflowing fullness or ample supply of material goods, food, energy, and resources.

CON-084
Cosmopolitan Justice: Moral Duties to Future Generations
Philosophy & Religion

Think about a sweet baby who will be born in your hometown one hundred years from now, in the year 2125! That future child will want to hike through a towering green forest, swim in crystal-clear rivers, and breathe fresh, crisp air. Because future generations cannot vote in our elections today, every living citizen must act as a brave and loving guardian of tomorrow!

Protecting our descendants requires that today's leaders consider the long-term impact of every law, avoiding nuclear waste dumps and preserving wild natural ecosystems for centuries to come. Passing laws that protect clean water for seven generations ensures that our descendants inherit a healthy, thriving planet. To champion the legal rights of future humans, students author a Charter for Future Generations and Institutional Design Kit with future-impact budget rules!
Guardian: A defender, protector, or keeper who looks after someone who cannot protect themselves.
Forest: A large area covered chiefly with trees and undergrowth, supporting biodiversity and cooling the climate.
Tomorrow: The future period of time, especially the world and environment that future generations will inherit.
Why do people living today have a moral duty to protect clean drinking water and fresh air for children who will be born 100 years from now?
How can passing laws with a 'seven-generation rule' help cities make wiser, kinder environmental choices?
If a community youth council plants 5 heritage oak trees each year for 6 years, how many trees will grow for the future? (5 × 6 = ___ trees)
Draw a majestic ancient oak tree providing cool shade for children playing in a clean, sunny future world, then write one pledge to protect the Earth for the future.

[Q1]: Actions taken today permanently shape the climate, oceans, and natural resources inherited by future children who have no say in current politics.
[Q2]: It requires decision-makers to ask whether a new road, factory, or law will still be good and safe for great-great-great-grandchildren.
[Q3]: 5 trees × 6 years = 30 heritage oak trees planted.
[Activity]: Drawings should show flourishing natural landscapes with future children; pledges should commit to conserving resources and planting trees.

Cosmopolitan justice and intergenerational ethics challenge contemporary democratic institutions to recognize moral duties to unborn generations who will inherit our planet in 2100 and beyond. Traditional democratic politics suffers from acute temporal bias: electoral cycles incentivize politicians to prioritize short-term voter benefits while shifting long-term existential costs—such as climate destabilization, biodiversity extinction, and toxic nuclear waste accumulation—onto future citizens who cannot vote. Furthermore, conventional economic cost-benefit models utilize discount rates that mathematically treat future human lives as having negligible economic value. Overcoming this injustice requires institutional innovation: establishing statutory 'Future Generations Commissioners' equipped with legislative veto powers, incorporating indigenous Seven-Generation principles into constitutional jurisprudence, and conducting mandatory 50-year intergenerational impact audits on all national infrastructure projects.
Cosmopolitan: Including people from many different countries or all humanity; recognizing all human beings as members of a single community.
Temporal: Relating to time; specifically the bias in politics toward immediate short-term events rather than long-term consequences.
Discount: An economic calculation rate used to determine the present value of future cash flows or future human costs.
Veto: A constitutional right to reject or block a decision, proposal, or piece of legislation made by a law-making body.
How does the economic 'pure rate of time preference' in discount rate formulas mathematically devalue the welfare of future human lives?
What statutory powers and legal standing does a 'Future Generations Commissioner' possess to block environmentally destructive legislation?
How do indigenous 'Seven-Generation' decision-making frameworks ensure that current community projects remain sustainable for 150 years into the future?

An intergenerational justice research foundation allocates ₱84,000 across 3 sectors: Future Generations Law, Intergenerational Audits, and Youth Ombudsmen. If ₱2,800 is reserved per sector, what is the net budget per program? (₱84,000 ÷ 3 - ₱2,800 = ?)
Draft a constitutional amendment bill establishing an independent Office of the Future Generations Commissioner with authority to review all national budgets and veto climate-harming laws.

[Q1]: Applying positive discount rates (e.g., 3-5%) reduces the calculated economic value of catastrophic climate harms 100 years from now to near zero.
[Q2]: Possesses legal standing to intervene in court actions, audit proposed long-term infrastructure budgets, and issue formal delays on harmful bills.
[Q3]: Mandates that before approving any major land use or resource policy, leaders must deliberate its impacts across seven future generations.
[Q4]: ₱84,000 ÷ 3 = ₱28,000. Net budget = ₱28,000 - ₱2,800 = ₱25,200 per intergenerational justice division.
[Rubric]: The draft amendment must define commissioner independence, statutory review standards, and binding legislative delay or veto powers.

The formal institutionalization of intergenerational cosmopolitan justice represents a profound frontier in constitutional jurisprudence, moral philosophy, and long-term risk assessment. Philosophers analyze the 'tyranny of the present,' showing that temporal asymmetry—wherein current generations hold absolute causal power over the future while bearing zero reciprocal consequences—violates the foundational social contract under John Rawls's 'veil of ignorance.' In legal theory, pioneering jurisdictions are establishing constitutional rights of future generations (e.g., the German Federal Constitutional Court's 2021 climate ruling) and granting legal personhood to rivers, recognizing that intergenerational liberty requires preserving the ecological preconditions of human existence. In risk engineering, safeguarding the deep future demands constructing 10,000-year semiotic warning systems for deep geological nuclear repositories (like Onkalo in Finland) and establishing resilient biodiversity vault networks that withstand multi-century sociopolitical collapses.
Asymmetry: A lack of equality or equivalence between two things, such as current generations having power over future generations with no reciprocation.
Veil: A conceptual boundary in moral philosophy (Rawls's Veil of Ignorance) where one designs rules without knowing where they will stand in society or time.
Semiotic: Relating to signs and symbols, used in engineering deep-time warning markers that can be understood across thousands of years.
Repository: A central storage facility or underground vault, specifically designed for deep geological disposal of high-level nuclear waste.
Explain how John Rawls's 'veil of ignorance' applies to intergenerational justice when deciding current planetary resource consumption rates.
What semiotic design principles (e.g., non-linguistic pictograms, menacing earthworks) are utilized to communicate radiation danger across 10,000 years at deep geological repositories?
How did the 2021 German Federal Constitutional Court climate ruling establish intergenerational fundamental rights by ruling that current inaction compromises future freedom?
Evaluate the moral philosophy debate: Does the non-identity problem diminish our moral duties to mitigate long-term existential and climate risks?

A long-term intergenerational policy center audits 350 national infrastructure proposals. If 50-year climate modeling expands review capacity by 14% in Year 1, and youth council vetting adds 12% in Year 2, find Year 2 audited proposals: (350 × 1.14 × 1.12).

Draft an executive constitutional amendment establishing an independent Fourth Branch of Government—the Guardian of Future Generations—with binding veto authority over national debt, environmental degradation, and long-term existential risk policies.

[Q1]: Parties behind the veil do not know which generation they will be born into, compelling them to choose fair, sustainable savings rates that protect all eras equally.
[Q2]: Replaces fragile written languages with universal morphological pictograms, bio-acoustic deterrents, and physical earthworks (e.g., thorn fields) indicating lethal toxicity.
[Q3]: Ruled that offloading drastic emissions reduction burdens onto future generations violates their fundamental constitutional liberties, requiring proactive mitigation now.
[Q4]: Non-identity asserts future individuals wouldn't exist without our choices; however, rights-based and threshold models establish duties to avoid leaving a devastated world.
[Q5]: Year 1 = 350 × 1.14 = 399 proposals. Year 2 = 399 × 1.12 = 446.88 (446 national proposals). Total gain = 96.88 proposals (+27.68%).
[Rubric]: The constitutional amendment must establish uncompromised judicial standing, an independent funding endowment, and explicit veto criteria over long-term existential threats.
